beats.text: A hospital buys a model that predicts which patients will deteriorate. In testing, it works beautifully.
Then it goes live on the wards, and the alerts start coming in.
But nobody decided who should respond. Should the nurse check the patient? Should a doctor order a test? Should someone call the intensive care team?
So the alert bounces around. Everyone sees it. No one owns it.
The result: more work for the staff, and no better outcomes for the patients. Knowing that a problem may happen is useful only if you can do something about it.
Prediction is only the beginning. Here are six steps from prediction to action.
One. Define the target exactly. Deterioration within six hours? Twenty-four hours? Seven days?
Two. Use only the information that exists at the moment of prediction. Peeking at data from the future is called leakage, and it makes results look unrealistically good.
Three. Estimate the risk with a validated model. A model that worked in another hospital still needs testing in yours.
Four. Choose a threshold. That decides who gets an alert.
Five. Link the alert to a response. Who does what, and how fast? For example: the nurse reviews the patient within thirty minutes.
Six. Measure the whole process. Did patient outcomes improve? Did unnecessary tests go up?
A good prediction with no response plan is just noise. The value comes from the decision it improves.
